claim: Chromosome instability (CIN) is deleterious to normal cells because of the burden of aneuploidy.
source: Chromosome instability (CIN) is deleterious to normal cells because of the burden of aneuploidy.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific understanding and citations in the introduction.

claim: Most human solid tumors have an abnormal karyotype.
source: However, most human solid tumors have an abnormal karyotype implying that gain and loss of chromosomes by cancer cells confers a selective advantage.
evidence: This is a well-established observation in cancer biology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Gain and loss of chromosomes by cancer cells confers a selective advantage.
source: However, most human solid tumors have an abnormal karyotype implying that gain and loss of chromosomes by cancer cells confers a selective advantage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most solid tumors have abnormal karyotypes.

claim: CIN can be induced in the mouse by inactivating the spindle assembly checkpoint.
source: CIN can be induced in the mouse by inactivating the spindle assembly checkpoint.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and the experimental approach described in the manuscript.

claim: Germline inactivation of the spindle assembly checkpoint is lethal in mice.
source: This is lethal in the germline but we show here that adult T cells and hepatocytes can survive conditional inactivation of the Mad2l1 SAC gene and resulting CIN.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and established knowledge.

claim: Adult T cells can survive conditional inactivation of the Mad2l1 SAC gene.
source: This is lethal in the germline but we show here that adult T cells and hepatocytes can survive conditional inactivation of the Mad2l1 SAC gene and resulting CIN.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript showing survival and tumor development in T cells with Mad2l1 deletion.

claim: Adult hepatocytes can survive conditional inactivation of the Mad2l1 SAC gene.
source: This is lethal in the germline but we show here that adult T cells and hepatocytes can survive conditional inactivation of the Mad2l1 SAC gene and resulting CIN.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the manuscript showing survival and tumor development in hepatocytes with Mad2l1 deletion.

claim: Conditional inactivation of Mad2l1 in T cells causes rapid onset of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL).
source: This causes rapid onset of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and progressive development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), both lethal diseases.
evidence: This is supported by survival data and histological analysis showing T-ALL development in Mad2l1-deleted mice.

claim: Conditional inactivation of Mad2l1 in hepatocytes causes progressive development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
source: This causes rapid onset of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and progressive development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), both lethal diseases.
evidence: This is supported by survival data, histological analysis, and MRI imaging showing HCC development in Mad2l1-deleted mice.

claim: T-ALL and HCC resulting from Mad2l1 deletion are lethal diseases.
source: This causes rapid onset of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and progressive development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), both lethal diseases.
evidence: This is supported by survival curves showing death of animals with these tumors.

claim: DNA copy number variation patterns are tumor-type specific in Mad2l1-deleted tumors.
source: The resulting DNA copy number variation and patterns of chromosome loss and gain are tumor-type specific, suggesting differential selective pressures on the two tumor cell types.
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data showing different patterns of chromosome gains and losses in T-ALL versus HCC.

claim: Patterns of chromosome loss and gain are tumor-type specific in Mad2l1-deleted tumors.
source: The resulting DNA copy number variation and patterns of chromosome loss and gain are tumor-type specific, suggesting differential selective pressures on the two tumor cell types.
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data showing different patterns of chromosome gains and losses in T-ALL versus HCC.

claim: Differential selective pressures act on T-ALL and HCC tumor cell types.
source: The resulting DNA copy number variation and patterns of chromosome loss and gain are tumor-type specific, suggesting differential selective pressures on the two tumor cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of tumor-type specific patterns of chromosome alterations.

claim: Aneuploidy is a hallmark of solid tumors.
source: Aneuploidy, the presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell, is a hallmark of solid tumors and in human cancers is frequently an indicator of poor prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and consensus in cancer biology.

claim: Aneuploidy in human cancers is frequently an indicator of poor prognosis.
source: Aneuploidy, the presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes in a cell, is a hallmark of solid tumors and in human cancers is frequently an indicator of poor prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and clinical observations.

claim: Genomic instability has the potential to promote loss of tumor suppressors.
source: Genomic instability has the potential to promote loss of tumor suppressors and increases in oncogene copy number, thereby driving tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific understanding of cancer biology.

claim: Genomic instability has the potential to promote increases in oncogene copy number.
source: Genomic instability has the potential to promote loss of tumor suppressors and increases in oncogene copy number, thereby driving tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific understanding of cancer biology.

claim: Genomic instability drives tumorigenesis.
source: Genomic instability has the potential to promote loss of tumor suppressors and increases in oncogene copy number, thereby driving tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific understanding and the experimental results in the manuscript.

claim: Chromosome imbalance imposes a physiological burden that reduces cell fitness.
source: However, experiments in non-transformed cells show that chromosome imbalance imposes a physiological burden that reduces cell fitness (Torres et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2008; Kops et al., 2004; Mao et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) engineered to carry an extra chromosome grow more slowly than wild-type cells.
source: Primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) engineered to carry an extra chromosome grow more slowly than wild-type cells and exhibit significant changes in metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by established experimental observations in the field.

claim: Primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) engineered to carry an extra chromosome exhibit significant changes in metabolism.
source: Primary murine embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) engineered to carry an extra chromosome grow more slowly than wild-type cells and exhibit significant changes in metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by established experimental observations in the field.

claim: Cells from Down syndrome patients carry a supernumerary chromosome 21.
source: The same is true of cells from Down syndrome patients, which carry a supernumerary chromosome 21 (Williams et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about Down syndrome supported by citations.

claim: Cells from Down syndrome patients exhibit reduced growth similar to aneuploid MEFs.
source: The same is true of cells from Down syndrome patients, which carry a supernumerary chromosome 21 (Williams et al., 2008; Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the context that 'the same is true' refers to the growth and metabolic changes described for aneuploid MEFs.

claim: Tumors may experience a burst of chromosome instability (CIN) leading to the emergence of clones with greater oncogenic potential.
source: It has been suggested that tumors experience a burst of chromosome instability (CIN) leading to the emergence of clones with greater oncogenic potential but that CIN is then suppressed so that cancer cells maintain a relatively stable karyotype (Lengauer et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: CIN is suppressed after an initial burst so that cancer cells maintain a relatively stable karyotype.
source: It has been suggested that tumors experience a burst of chromosome instability (CIN) leading to the emergence of clones with greater oncogenic potential but that CIN is then suppressed so that cancer cells maintain a relatively stable karyotype (Lengauer et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations, referred to as the 'genome restabilization' model.

claim: The model of 'genome restabilization' is supported by statistical analysis of tumor karyotype across large numbers of human cancer genomes.
source: This model of 'genome restabilization' is supported by statistical analysis of tumor karyotype across large numbers of human cancer genomes including identification of a common cancer karyotype, overlaid by tissue-specific differences, in genomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (Davoli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to analysis of TCGA data.

claim: A common cancer karyotype exists, overlaid by tissue-specific differences.
source: This model of 'genome restabilization' is supported by statistical analysis of tumor karyotype across large numbers of human cancer genomes including identification of a common cancer karyotype, overlaid by tissue-specific differences, in genomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (Davoli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to analysis of TCGA data.

claim: Aneuploidy appears most common in areas of the genome having more oncogenes and tumor suppressors.
source: In addition, aneuploidy appears most common in areas of the genome having more oncogenes and tumor suppressors, implying positive selection.
evidence: This is an observation from genomic analysis that implies positive selection.

claim: The distribution of aneuploidy in the genome implies positive selection.
source: In addition, aneuploidy appears most common in areas of the genome having more oncogenes and tumor suppressors, implying positive selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that aneuploidy is enriched in regions with oncogenes and tumor suppressors.

claim: Many solid tumors are genetically heterogeneous.
source: Conversely, however, many solid tumors are genetically heterogeneous, suggesting that CIN is not fully suppressed in growing tumors (Nicholson and Cimini, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature on tumor heterogeneity.

claim: Genetic heterogeneity in solid tumors suggests that CIN is not fully suppressed in growing tumors.
source: Conversely, however, many solid tumors are genetically heterogeneous, suggesting that CIN is not fully suppressed in growing tumors (Nicholson and Cimini, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of genetic heterogeneity.

claim: Mouse models of CIN provide an excellent tool for studying the role of aneuploidy in tumorigenesis.
source: Mouse models of CIN provide an excellent tool for studying the role of aneuploidy in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the experimental approach used in the manuscript.

claim: One method to induce CIN is to disrupt the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC).
source: One method to induce CIN is to disrupt the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC).
evidence: This is the experimental approach used in the manuscript and is supported by established knowledge.

claim: The SAC senses the presence of maloriented or detached kinetochores.
source: The SAC senses the presence of maloriented or detached kinetochores and blocks exit from mitosis until pairs of sister chromatids achieve the bipolar geometry that is uniquely compatible with normal chromosome disjunction (Jallepalli and Lengauer, 2001; Taylor et al., 2004; Rieder et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAC function supported by citations.

claim: The SAC blocks exit from mitosis until pairs of sister chromatids achieve the bipolar geometry compatible with normal chromosome disjunction.
source: The SAC senses the presence of maloriented or detached kinetochores and blocks exit from mitosis until pairs of sister chromatids achieve the bipolar geometry that is uniquely compatible with normal chromosome disjunction (Jallepalli and Lengauer, 2001; Taylor et al., 2004; Rieder et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge about SAC function supported by citations.

claim: Germline deletion of murine SAC genes is lethal by ~E10.5.
source: Studying the SAC in mice is complicated by the fact that germline deletion of murine SAC genes is lethal by ~E10.5 (Li et al., 2009; Dobles et al., 2000; Babu et al., 2003; Baker et al., 2004; García-Higuera et al., 2008; Iwanaga et al., 2007; Perera et al., 2007; Putkey et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Most studies of SAC knockouts to date have employed heterozygous animals or hypomorphic alleles.
source: As a result, most studies of SAC knockouts to date have employed heterozygous animals or hypomorphic alleles, resulting in weak and sporadic tumor development at long latencies (Iwanaga et al., 2007; Burds et al., 2005; Dai et al., 2004; Michel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Heterozygous SAC knockout animals or hypomorphic alleles result in weak and sporadic tumor development at long latencies.
source: As a result, most studies of SAC knockouts to date have employed heterozygous animals or hypomorphic alleles, resulting in weak and sporadic tumor development at long latencies (Iwanaga et al., 2007; Burds et al., 2005; Dai et al., 2004; Michel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of Mad2l1 is tolerated by murine interfollicular epidermal cells.
source: We have previously shown that deletion of Mad2l1 (HUGO MD2L1; UniProt Q9Z1B5), an essential component of the SAC, is tolerated by murine interfollicular epidermal cells, which terminally differentiate to form the outer layers of the skin, but not by hair follicle bulge stem cells, a specialized self-renewing cell type required for hair follicle maintenance (Foijer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Deletion of Mad2l1 is not tolerated by hair follicle bulge stem cells.
source: We have previously shown that deletion of Mad2l1 (HUGO MD2L1; UniProt Q9Z1B5), an essential component of the SAC, is tolerated by murine interfollicular epidermal cells, which terminally differentiate to form the outer layers of the skin, but not by hair follicle bulge stem cells, a specialized self-renewing cell type required for hair follicle maintenance (Foijer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Murine interfollicular epidermal cells terminally differentiate to form the outer layers of the skin.
source: We have previously shown that deletion of Mad2l1 (HUGO MD2L1; UniProt Q9Z1B5), an essential component of the SAC, is tolerated by murine interfollicular epidermal cells, which terminally differentiate to form the outer layers of the skin, but not by hair follicle bulge stem cells, a specialized self-renewing cell type required for hair follicle maintenance (Foijer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about skin cell biology.

claim: Hair follicle bulge stem cells are a specialized self-renewing cell type required for hair follicle maintenance.
source: We have previously shown that deletion of Mad2l1 (HUGO MD2L1; UniProt Q9Z1B5), an essential component of the SAC, is tolerated by murine interfollicular epidermal cells, which terminally differentiate to form the outer layers of the skin, but not by hair follicle bulge stem cells, a specialized self-renewing cell type required for hair follicle maintenance (Foijer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hair follicle biology.

claim: A functional SAC is required in cells undergoing repeated division.
source: These findings support the idea that a functional SAC is required in cells undergoing repeated division, but not necessarily in differentiated cells with limited proliferative potential.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SAC deletion is tolerated in terminally differentiating cells but not in self-renewing stem cells.

claim: A functional SAC is not necessarily required in differentiated cells with limited proliferative potential.
source: These findings support the idea that a functional SAC is required in cells undergoing repeated division, but not necessarily in differentiated cells with limited proliferative potential.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SAC deletion is tolerated in terminally differentiating cells.

claim: Cancers grow from one or a small number of cells which must divide many times to create a macroscopic tumor.
source: The implications for cancer are unclear, since cancers grow from one or a small number of cells which must divide many times to create a macroscopic tumor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Conditional deletions or mutations in Trp53 were introduced to tolerize cells to checkpoint loss.
source: To tolerize cells to checkpoint loss we also introduced conditional deletions or mutations in Trp53.
evidence: This is part of the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: Trp53 mutations promote oncogenesis.
source: We found that T-cells and hepatocytes survive checkpoint loss in both the presence and absence of Trp53 mutation but that Trp53 mutations promote oncogenesis (Jacks et al., 1994; Purdie et al., 1994; Donehower et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citations to previous studies.

claim: T-cells survive checkpoint loss in both the presence and absence of Trp53 mutation.
source: We found that T-cells and hepatocytes survive checkpoint loss in both the presence and absence of Trp53 mutation but that Trp53 mutations promote oncogenesis (Jacks et al., 1994; Purdie et al., 1994; Donehower et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing survival of T-cells with Mad2l1 deletion in different Trp53 backgrounds.

claim: Hepatocytes survive checkpoint loss in both the presence and absence of Trp53 mutation.
source: We found that T-cells and hepatocytes survive checkpoint loss in both the presence and absence of Trp53 mutation but that Trp53 mutations promote oncogenesis (Jacks et al., 1994; Purdie et al., 1994; Donehower et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing survival of hepatocytes with Mad2l1 deletion in different Trp53 backgrounds.

claim: Loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 in T-cells causes rapidly growing acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL).
source: In T-cells, loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 causes rapidly growing acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and in hepatocytes it causes progressive disease that ends in lethal hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
evidence: This is supported by survival data and tumor characterization in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 in hepatocytes causes progressive disease that ends in lethal hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
source: In T-cells, loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 causes rapidly growing acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and in hepatocytes it causes progressive disease that ends in lethal hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
evidence: This is supported by survival data, histological analysis, and MRI imaging in the manuscript.

claim: Mad2l1-null T-ALLs experienced an elevated rate of chromosome mis-segregation relative to normal T cells.
source: Single-cell sequencing shows that Mad2l1-null T-ALLs experienced an elevated rate of chromosome mis-segregation relative to normal T cells and murine T-cells in which the SAC is partially inactivated by truncation of Mps1 (Mps1 is another SAC component; (Bakker et al., 2016; Foijer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell sequencing data showing extensive aneuploidy and heterogeneity in T-ALLs.

claim: Mad2l1-null T-ALLs experienced an elevated rate of chromosome mis-segregation relative to murine T-cells in which the SAC is partially inactivated by truncation of Mps1.
source: Single-cell sequencing shows that Mad2l1-null T-ALLs experienced an elevated rate of chromosome mis-segregation relative to normal T cells and murine T-cells in which the SAC is partially inactivated by truncation of Mps1 (Mps1 is another SAC component; (Bakker et al., 2016; Foijer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell sequencing data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Mad2l1-null T-ALLs and HCCs assayed at a population level using aCGH show recurrent and tissue-specific patterns of chromosome loss and gain.
source: In contrast, when Mad2l1-null T-ALLs and HCCs were assayed at a population level using array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) recurrent and tissue-specific patterns of chromosome loss and gain were observed.
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data showing specific patterns of chromosome alterations in different tumor types.

claim: LoxP sites were inserted upstream of exon 2 and downstream of exon 5 of Mad2l1.
source: LoxP sites were inserted upstream of exon 2 and downstream of exon 5 so that Cre expression would result in deletion of ~90% of the Mad2l1 ORF (Mad2l1Δ; Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is part of the experimental design shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Cre expression results in deletion of ~90% of the Mad2l1 ORF.
source: LoxP sites were inserted upstream of exon 2 and downstream of exon 5 so that Cre expression would result in deletion of ~90% of the Mad2l1 ORF (Mad2l1Δ; Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on the design of the conditional allele shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Correct targeting of the Mad2l1 construct in ES cells was confirmed by Southern blotting.
source: Correct targeting of the construct in ES cells was confirmed by Southern blotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the Southern blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Crossing Mad2l1f and Lck-Cre transgenic animals induces recombination of Mad2l1f in CD4– CD8– T cells.
source: By crossing Mad2l1f and Lck-Cre transgenic animals we induced recombination of Mad2l1f in CD4– CD8– T cells (Molina et al., 1992) and by crossing with Alb-Cre carrying mice we induced Mad2l1f recombination in developing hepatocytes (Weisend et al., 2009), a post-mitotic cell type that normally exhibits polyloidy (Duncan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is part of the experimental design supported by citation to the Lck-Cre system.

claim: Crossing Mad2l1f and Alb-Cre carrying mice induces Mad2l1f recombination in developing hepatocytes.
source: By crossing Mad2l1f and Lck-Cre transgenic animals we induced recombination of Mad2l1f in CD4– CD8– T cells (Molina et al., 1992) and by crossing with Alb-Cre carrying mice we induced Mad2l1f recombination in developing hepatocytes (Weisend et al., 2009), a post-mitotic cell type that normally exhibits polyloidy (Duncan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is part of the experimental design supported by citation to the Alb-Cre system.

claim: Hepatocytes are a post-mitotic cell type that normally exhibits polyploidy.
source: By crossing Mad2l1f and Lck-Cre transgenic animals we induced recombination of Mad2l1f in CD4– CD8– T cells (Molina et al., 1992) and by crossing with Alb-Cre carrying mice we induced Mad2l1f recombination in developing hepatocytes (Weisend et al., 2009), a post-mitotic cell type that normally exhibits polyloidy (Duncan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hepatocyte biology supported by citation.

claim: Mad2l1 excision was efficient in both T cells and hepatocytes.
source: In both tissues, genotyping showed that Mad2l1 excision was efficient (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Trp53 loss promotes survival of Mad2l1-deficient murine cells.
source: We generated a tumor-sensitized background by crossing Cre transgenic Mad2l1f/fand FLOX-Trp53 (Trp53f) mice (Jonkers et al., 2001); Trp53 loss has been shown to promote survival of Mad2l1-deficient murine cells (Burds et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice did not experience malignancies within the first year of life.
source: Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice did not experience malignancies within the first year of life (Figure 1D) and adult T cells from these animals developed normally, suggesting that T cells are tolerant of Mad2l1 loss.
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Adult T cells from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ animals developed normally.
source: Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice did not experience malignancies within the first year of life (Figure 1D) and adult T cells from these animals developed normally, suggesting that T cells are tolerant of Mad2l1 loss.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: T cells are tolerant of Mad2l1 loss.
source: Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice did not experience malignancies within the first year of life (Figure 1D) and adult T cells from these animals developed normally, suggesting that T cells are tolerant of Mad2l1 loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that T cells develop normally in the absence of Mad2l1.

claim: Loss of Mad2l1 on a Trp53-heterozygous background resulted in death of ~50% of animals by ~8 mo. from T-ALL.
source: On a Trp53-heterozygous background (a Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/+ genotype) loss of Mad2l1 resulted in death of ~50% of animals by ~8 mo. (from T-ALL, see below) whereas control animals heterozygous for a Trp53 deletion but carrying wild type Mad2l1 had the same lifespan as wild-type littermate controls (Figure 1D; blue lines, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Control animals heterozygous for a Trp53 deletion but carrying wild type Mad2l1 had the same lifespan as wild-type littermate controls.
source: On a Trp53-heterozygous background (a Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/+ genotype) loss of Mad2l1 resulted in death of ~50% of animals by ~8 mo. (from T-ALL, see below) whereas control animals heterozygous for a Trp53 deletion but carrying wild type Mad2l1 had the same lifespan as wild-type littermate controls (Figure 1D; blue lines, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Loss of Mad2l1 on a Trp53-homozygous deletion background resulted in rapid disease progression with half of double mutant animals dead by ~4 mo.
source: On a Trp53-homozygous deletion background, loss of Mad2l1 (i.e. an Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f genotype) resulted in rapid disease progression with half of double mutant animals dead by ~4 mo. (Figure 1D; red line).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Double mutant mice (Mad2l1 and Trp53 deletion) experienced a statistically significant acceleration in cancer development relative to mice homozygous for Trp53 deletion.
source: Double mutant mice experienced a statistically significant acceleration in cancer development relative to mice homozygous for Trp53 deletion, which itself is known to be highly tumorigenic in thymocytes (Figure 1D; compare green and red lines, p<0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of survival data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Trp53 deletion is highly tumorigenic in thymocytes.
source: Double mutant mice experienced a statistically significant acceleration in cancer development relative to mice homozygous for Trp53 deletion, which itself is known to be highly tumorigenic in thymocytes (Figure 1D; compare green and red lines, p<0.01).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the survival data.

claim: Dyspnea (labored breathing) was observed shortly before the death of Mad2l1-mutant animals.
source: Dyspnea (labored breathing) was observed shortly before the death of Mad2l1-mutant animals, consistent with thymic hypertrophy.
evidence: This is a clinical observation from the animal experiments.

claim: Dyspnea in Mad2l1-mutant animals is consistent with thymic hypertrophy.
source: Dyspnea (labored breathing) was observed shortly before the death of Mad2l1-mutant animals, consistent with thymic hypertrophy.
evidence: This is inferred from the clinical presentation and the observed thymic enlargement.

claim: Post-mortem analysis of Mad2l1-mutant tissues revealed a ~10–15 fold increase in the average mass of the thymus.
source: Post-mortem analysis of tissues revealed a ~10–15 fold increase in the average mass of the thymus and 70% increase in the mass of the spleen (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Post-mortem analysis of Mad2l1-mutant tissues revealed a 70% increase in the mass of the spleen.
source: Post-mortem analysis of tissues revealed a ~10–15 fold increase in the average mass of the thymus and 70% increase in the mass of the spleen (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Histological analysis of thymi from Mad2l1-mutant animals demonstrated the presence of rapidly dividing blasts with irregular nuclei and abnormal DNA.
source: Histological analysis of thymi demonstrated the presence of rapidly dividing blasts with irregular nuclei and abnormal DNA, consistent with lymphoma (Figure 1G, compare top and bottom panels).
evidence: This is supported by H&E staining shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The histological features of Mad2l1-mutant thymi are consistent with lymphoma.
source: Histological analysis of thymi demonstrated the presence of rapidly dividing blasts with irregular nuclei and abnormal DNA, consistent with lymphoma (Figure 1G, compare top and bottom panels).
evidence: This is inferred from the histological features observed.

claim: Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss cooperate in oncogenic transformation of T-cells.
source: We conclude that Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss cooperate in oncogenic transformation of T-cells and that the combination is rapidly lethal.
evidence: This is concluded from the survival and tumor data showing accelerated disease in double mutants.

claim: The combination of Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss is rapidly lethal.
source: We conclude that Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss cooperate in oncogenic transformation of T-cells and that the combination is rapidly lethal.
evidence: This is supported by survival data showing death within 4 months.

claim: Thymi from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals euthanized prior to dyspnea contained numerous dividing and undifferentiated (blasting) cells.
source: To characterize cellular defects in double knockout mice, ~20 Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals were euthanized prior to the appearance of dyspnea and thymocytes then analyzed. FACS showed that thymi from these animals contained numerous dividing and undifferentiated (blasting) cells in comparison to thymi from control animals (Figure 1H; blasts, red arrow, normal cells black arrow).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: In ~10% of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals thymi were macroscopically normal but contained an abnormal number of dividing and undifferentiated cells.
source: In ~10% of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals thymi were macroscopically normal but they also contained an abnormal number of dividing and undifferentiated cells showing that this phenotype was fully penetrant.
evidence: This is an observation from the FACS analysis of multiple animals.

claim: The blasting cell phenotype in Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals was fully penetrant.
source: In ~10% of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals thymi were macroscopically normal but they also contained an abnormal number of dividing and undifferentiated cells showing that this phenotype was fully penetrant.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that even macroscopically normal thymi showed the phenotype.

claim: In most Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals, the spleen contained blasting cells and was enlarged.
source: In most animals, the spleen also contained blasting cells and was enlarged, suggesting metastasis of T-cells to this organ (Figure 1H compare blasting population highlighted by red arrow in lower right panel with blasting cells in thymus).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Blasting cells in the spleen of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals suggest metastasis of T-cells to this organ.
source: In most animals, the spleen also contained blasting cells and was enlarged, suggesting metastasis of T-cells to this organ (Figure 1H compare blasting population highlighted by red arrow in lower right panel with blasting cells in thymus).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of similar blasting cells in both thymus and spleen.

claim: Blasts were not observed in the peripheral blood of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals.
source: However, blasts were not observed in the peripheral blood (Figure 1H bottom center panel).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The majority of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals suffered from poorly differentiated CD4+ and CD8+ T-acute lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-ALL).
source: These and related data show that the majority of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals suffered from poorly differentiated CD4+ and CD8+ T-acute lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-ALL) while a subset suffer from more differentiated CD4+ or CD8+ T-ALL as described previously for Trp53null thymic lymphoma (Donehower et al., 1995).
evidence: This is concluded from FACS and histological analysis of multiple animals.

claim: A subset of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals suffer from more differentiated CD4+ or CD8+ T-ALL.
source: These and related data show that the majority of Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals suffered from poorly differentiated CD4+ and CD8+ T-acute lymphoblastic lymphoma (T-ALL) while a subset suffer from more differentiated CD4+ or CD8+ T-ALL as described previously for Trp53null thymic lymphoma (Donehower et al., 1995).
evidence: This is concluded from FACS analysis and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) analysis of TCR α and β loci revealed a single dominant rearranged TCR in each animal.
source: Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) analysis of TCR α and β loci on chromosomes 14 and 6 revealed a single dominant rearranged TCR in each animal implying that T-ALLs were clonal (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2, array CGH data was deposited at GSE63686 in NCBI GEO).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: T-ALLs in Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals were clonal.
source: Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) analysis of TCR α and β loci on chromosomes 14 and 6 revealed a single dominant rearranged TCR in each animal implying that T-ALLs were clonal (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2, array CGH data was deposited at GSE63686 in NCBI GEO).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of a single dominant TCR rearrangement.

claim: Mad2l1-null T-ALL tumors grow large enough to kill animals while remaining clonal at TCR loci.
source: In sum, these data demonstrate synergy between loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 in the transformation of T-cells to malignant T-ALL and show that tumors grow large enough to kill animals while remaining clonal at TCR loci.
evidence: This is concluded from the combination of survival data and TCR clonality analysis.

claim: Mad2l1-null cells must proliferate extensively subsequent to a tumor-initiating genetic event.
source: Mad2l1-null cells must therefore proliferate extensively subsequent to a tumor-initiating genetic event (a common characteristic of cancer).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that clonal tumors grow to macroscopic size.

claim: The lifespan of Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice was unchanged relative to wild-type littermates.
source: The lifespan of animals carrying a conditional knockout of Mad2l1 in hepatocytes (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice) was unchanged relative to wild-type littermates (Figure 2A) but double mutant animals deleted for Mad2l1 and one or both Trp53 alleles (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/+ and Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f mice) died significantly younger than littermate Mad2l1+/+::Trp53+/+ controls (p<0.01 and p<0.001 respectively).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Double mutant animals deleted for Mad2l1 and one or both Trp53 alleles died significantly younger than littermate controls.
source: The lifespan of animals carrying a conditional knockout of Mad2l1 in hepatocytes (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice) was unchanged relative to wild-type littermates (Figure 2A) but double mutant animals deleted for Mad2l1 and one or both Trp53 alleles (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/+ and Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f mice) died significantly younger than littermate Mad2l1+/+::Trp53+/+ controls (p<0.01 and p<0.001 respectively).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A with statistical analysis.

claim: Liver-specific deletion of one or both Trp53 alleles in Mad2l1-wild type animals had no detectable impact on lifespan.
source: In contrast, liver-specific deletion of one or both Trp53 alleles in Mad2l1-wild type animals had no detectable impact on lifespan (Figure 2A; Trp53f/+ blue lines, p<0.01; Trp53f/f red and green lines, p<0.001) consistent with previous data showing that Trp53 loss is only mildly oncogenic in hepatocytes (Harvey et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A and citation to previous work.

claim: Trp53 loss is only mildly oncogenic in hepatocytes.
source: In contrast, liver-specific deletion of one or both Trp53 alleles in Mad2l1-wild type animals had no detectable impact on lifespan (Figure 2A; Trp53f/+ blue lines, p<0.01; Trp53f/f red and green lines, p<0.001) consistent with previous data showing that Trp53 loss is only mildly oncogenic in hepatocytes (Harvey et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and the survival data.

claim: Post-mortem analysis of Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f and Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/+ animals revealed the presence of one or more liver tumors per mouse.
source: Post-mortem analysis of Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f and Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/+ animals revealed the presence of one or more liver tumors per mouse.
evidence: This is an observation from post-mortem examination of animals.

claim: In many cases liver tumors in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals were so large and invasive that the tri-lobular structure of the liver was unrecognizable.
source: In many cases these tumors were so large and invasive that the tri-lobular structure of the liver was unrecognizable (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by gross pathology images shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Widespread liver damage and formation of regenerative nodules was evident in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f animals by ~4 mo. of age.
source: In the case of single-mutant Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f animals, widespread liver damage and formation of regenerative nodules was evident by ~4 mo. of age.
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis at different time points.

claim: Regenerative nodules are non-neoplastic sites of liver proliferation and repair commonly present following liver damage.
source: Regenerative nodules are non-neoplastic sites of liver proliferation and repair commonly present following liver damage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about liver pathology.

claim: By 8–12 mo. of age benign hepatocellular adenoma (HCA) was evident in >50% of Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f animals.
source: By 8–12 mo. of age benign hepatocellular adenoma (HCA) was evident in >50% of animals (~5% of wild type animals also had HCA, which is normal for this genetic background [Leenders et al., 2008]) and by 12–16 mo. half of mice had hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: ~5% of wild type animals had HCA, which is normal for this genetic background.
source: By 8–12 mo. of age benign hepatocellular adenoma (HCA) was evident in >50% of animals (~5% of wild type animals also had HCA, which is normal for this genetic background [Leenders et al., 2008]) and by 12–16 mo. half of mice had hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on this genetic background.

claim: By 12–16 mo. half of Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f mice had hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
source: By 8–12 mo. of age benign hepatocellular adenoma (HCA) was evident in >50% of animals (~5% of wild type animals also had HCA, which is normal for this genetic background [Leenders et al., 2008]) and by 12–16 mo. half of mice had hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2D.

claim: Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f mice experienced benign and malignant liver cancer at high penetrance.
source: Thus Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f mice experienced benign and malignant liver cancer at high penetrance.
evidence: This is concluded from the high incidence of HCA and HCC in these animals.

claim: Deletion of Trp53 in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f animals dramatically accelerated the onset of cancer.
source: Deletion of Trp53 on this background (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals; Figure 2D) dramatically accelerated the onset of cancer, with 75% of 8–12 mo. old animals exhibiting HCC, occasionally in combination with HCA or cholangiocarcinoma (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the incidence data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1.

claim: 75% of 8–12 mo. old Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals exhibited HCC.
source: Deletion of Trp53 on this background (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals; Figure 2D) dramatically accelerated the onset of cancer, with 75% of 8–12 mo. old animals exhibiting HCC, occasionally in combination with HCA or cholangiocarcinoma (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the incidence data in Table 1.

claim: HCC in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals occasionally occurred in combination with HCA or cholangiocarcinoma.
source: Deletion of Trp53 on this background (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals; Figure 2D) dramatically accelerated the onset of cancer, with 75% of 8–12 mo. old animals exhibiting HCC, occasionally in combination with HCA or cholangiocarcinoma (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the incidence data in Table 1.

claim: The reduction in the proportion of HCC in older Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f mice arises because tumor-bearing animals die at an accelerated rate leaving behind disease-free animals.
source: Note that the reduction in the proportion of HCC Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/fmice in the cohort older than 16 mo. arises simply because tumor-bearing animals die at an accelerated rate leaving behind disease-free animals.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern in the incidence data.

claim: Nearly all Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals eventually get HCC.
source: This is less obvious for Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals because nearly all of them eventually get HCC (so increasing death is matched by increasing disease prevalence).
evidence: This is concluded from the high penetrance of HCC in these animals.

claim: People living in areas of the globe in which hepatotoxic agents are endemic often suffer from HCC that involves a dominant-negative Trp53-R249S mutation.
source: People living in areas of the globe in which hepatotoxic agents are endemic often suffer from HCC that involves a dominant-negative Trp53-R249S mutation (Yin et al., 1998; Hsu et al., 1991; Lee and Sabapathy, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human HCC supported by citations.

claim: Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53R246S mice (carrying the murine analog of the human Trp53-R249S mutation) experienced early death and extensive HCC.
source: When we crossed the murine analog of this mutation (Trp53-R246S) into Mad2l1-mutant animals (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53R246S mice; [Yin et al., 1998]) we observed early death and extensive HCC (Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53R246S vs. Alb-Cre:Trp53R246S littermates; p<0.001; compare Figure 2A and E, red lines).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53R246S mice recapitulate a known feature of human disease.
source: Such animals therefore recapitulate a known feature of human disease.
evidence: This is concluded from the similarity to human HCC with Trp53-R249S mutations.

claim: Mad2l1 deletion in hepatocytes is sufficient to cause HCC.
source: We conclude that Mad2l1 deletion in hepatocytes is sufficient to cause HCC but that tumor formation is significantly accelerated by deletion of Trp53 or introduction of a mouse analog of a Trp53 mutation commonly observed in human liver cancer.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f animals develop HCC.

claim: Tumor formation in Mad2l1-deleted hepatocytes is significantly accelerated by deletion of Trp53.
source: We conclude that Mad2l1 deletion in hepatocytes is sufficient to cause HCC but that tumor formation is significantly accelerated by deletion of Trp53 or introduction of a mouse analog of a Trp53 mutation commonly observed in human liver cancer.
evidence: This is supported by the survival and incidence data comparing different genotypes.

claim: Tumor formation in Mad2l1-deleted hepatocytes is significantly accelerated by introduction of a mouse analog of a Trp53 mutation commonly observed in human liver cancer.
source: We conclude that Mad2l1 deletion in hepatocytes is sufficient to cause HCC but that tumor formation is significantly accelerated by deletion of Trp53 or introduction of a mouse analog of a Trp53 mutation commonly observed in human liver cancer.
evidence: This is supported by the survival data for Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53R246S mice.

claim: EOVIST-excluding regions in MRI were confirmed to be tumors by fixing livers immediately after MRI followed by serial sectioning and H&E histology.
source: EOVIST-excluding regions were confirmed to be tumors by fixing livers immediately after MRI followed by serial sectioning and H&E histology of the same region of the tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the workflow shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tumor volume in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals increased approximately exponentially.
source: In nine animals examined (a total of 32 tumors) we observed that tumor volume increased approximately exponentially (Figure 2F,G) with an average doubling time of ~28 days (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by MRI measurements shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: The average doubling time of tumors in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals was ~28 days.
source: In nine animals examined (a total of 32 tumors) we observed that tumor volume increased approximately exponentially (Figure 2F,G) with an average doubling time of ~28 days (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The number of tumors in each Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animal increased with age.
source: Moreover, imaging revealed that the number of tumors in each animal increased with age so that by 12 mo. an average of 3 morphologically distinct tumors were present in each animal (range 1–7; n = 9).
evidence: This is supported by MRI imaging data.

claim: By 12 mo. an average of 3 morphologically distinct tumors were present in each Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animal.
source: Moreover, imaging revealed that the number of tumors in each animal increased with age so that by 12 mo. an average of 3 morphologically distinct tumors were present in each animal (range 1–7; n = 9).
evidence: This is supported by MRI imaging data.

claim: Liver cancer induced by loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 results in progressive multi-focal cancer.
source: We conclude that liver cancer induced by loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 results in progressive multi-focal cancer and that tumors grow exponentially once established.
evidence: This is concluded from the MRI data showing multiple tumors that increase in number and size over time.

claim: Tumors in Mad2l1 and Trp53 deleted livers grow exponentially once established.
source: We conclude that liver cancer induced by loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 results in progressive multi-focal cancer and that tumors grow exponentially once established.
evidence: This is concluded from the exponential growth curves observed by MRI.

claim: Liver cancer induced by loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 resembles human HCC, which is also multi-focal and progressive.
source: This resembles human HCC, which is also multi-focal and progressive.
evidence: This is a comparison to established knowledge about human HCC.

claim: Partially inactivating the SAC via truncation of Mps1 in T-cells accelerates Trp53-induced lymphomagenesis.
source: Although we have previously shown that partially inactivating the SAC via truncation of Mps1 in T-cells accelerates Trp53-induced lymphomagenesis (Foijer et al., 2014), the observation that Mad2l1-null T-ALLs and HCCs can grow rapidly is surprising.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The observation that Mad2l1-null T-ALLs and HCCs can grow rapidly is surprising.
source: Although we have previously shown that partially inactivating the SAC via truncation of Mps1 in T-cells accelerates Trp53-induced lymphomagenesis (Foijer et al., 2014), the observation that Mad2l1-null T-ALLs and HCCs can grow rapidly is surprising.
evidence: This is a statement about the unexpected nature of the findings given previous knowledge.

claim: Germline deletion of murine Mad2l1 is lethal.
source: Germline deletion of murine Mad2l1 is lethal and RNAi-mediated depletion of Mad2l1 in cancer cells results in mitotic catastrophe and cell death within approximately six cell doublings (Kops et al., 2004; Dobles et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of Mad2l1 in cancer cells results in mitotic catastrophe and cell death within approximately six cell doublings.
source: Germline deletion of murine Mad2l1 is lethal and RNAi-mediated depletion of Mad2l1 in cancer cells results in mitotic catastrophe and cell death within approximately six cell doublings (Kops et al., 2004; Dobles et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In all but one T-ALL tumor from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals, Mad2l1 DNA, mRNA, and protein were below the level of detection.
source: In all but one T-ALL tumor from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals (tumor 33, in which switching was incomplete and protein present) Mad2l1 DNA, mRNA, and protein were below the level of detection.
evidence: This is supported by genomic PCR, aCGH, qPCR, and Western blotting data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In tumor 33 from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals, switching was incomplete and Mad2l1 protein was present.
source: In all but one T-ALL tumor from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals (tumor 33, in which switching was incomplete and protein present) Mad2l1 DNA, mRNA, and protein were below the level of detection.
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PCR of HCCs from Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals revealed bands corresponding to both recombined and unrecombined Mad2l1.
source: In the case of HCCs from Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals, PCR revealed bands corresponding to both recombined and unrecombined Mad2l1 (Mad2l1Δ and Mad2l1f).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Probe values by aCGH in HCCs were generally intermediate between probe values for wild-type cells and Mad2l1-null T-ALLs.
source: Probe values by aCGH were generally intermediate between probe values for wild-type cells and Mad2l1-null T-ALLs (compare Figure 3B to Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 3B and E.

claim: The presence in HCC DNA of recombined and unrecombined Mad2l1f loci is expected since liver comprises multiple cell types and tumors contain high levels of infiltrating Mad2l1-proficient immune cells.
source: The presence in HCC DNA from recombined and unrecombined Mad2l1f loci is expected since liver comprises multiple cell types and tumors contain high levels of infiltrating Mad2l1-proficient immune cells.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed PCR and aCGH results based on tissue composition.

claim: Mad2l1-null HCCs were invasive so resected tumors were invariably contaminated with surrounding normal tissue.
source: Mad2l1-null HCCs were invasive so resected tumors were invariably contaminated with surrounding normal tissue (including tissue in which recombination might have been incomplete).
evidence: This is an observation from tumor dissection and an explanation for mixed genotypes.

claim: In a subset of HCCs, Mad2l1Δ was the dominant PCR product.
source: It is difficult to estimate the contribution of such cells to PCR signals, but in a subset of HCCs, Mad2l1Δ was the dominant PCR product (tumors in lanes 6 and 11 in Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Germline Mad2l1 heterozygosity did not cause HCC either alone or in combination with Trp53 deletion.
source: However, germline Mad2l1 heterozygosity did not cause HCC either alone or in combination with Trp53 deletion and we therefore find this explanation less likely (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the incidence data in Table 1.

claim: Mad2l1 protein and mRNA are present in amounts below the level of detection in virtually all T-ALLs.
source: Overall we conclude that Mad2l1 protein and mRNA are present in amounts below the level of detection in virtually all T-ALLs and that in some HCCs, the extent of recombination is sufficiently high that some, and perhaps all transformed hepatocytes lack a functional Mad2l1 gene.
evidence: This is concluded from the PCR, qPCR, and Western blotting data.

claim: In some HCCs, the extent of recombination is sufficiently high that some, and perhaps all transformed hepatocytes lack a functional Mad2l1 gene.
source: Overall we conclude that Mad2l1 protein and mRNA are present in amounts below the level of detection in virtually all T-ALLs and that in some HCCs, the extent of recombination is sufficiently high that some, and perhaps all transformed hepatocytes lack a functional Mad2l1 gene.
evidence: This is concluded from the PCR and aCGH data showing high levels of recombination in some HCCs.

claim: Addition of Dox to Mad2l1f/f MEFs that express Dox-Cre resulted in efficient excision of Mad2l1.
source: Addition of Dox to Mad2l1f/f MEFs that express Dox-Cre resulted in efficient excision of Mad2l1 as judged by PCR genotyping and Western blotting for Mad2l1 protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by PCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mad2l1-null MEFs could be passaged multiple times in low oxygen conditions.
source: The resulting Mad2l1-null MEFs could be passaged multiple times in low oxygen conditions.
evidence: This is an observation from cell culture experiments.

claim: Exposure of wild-type MEFs to nocodazole for 6 hr. increased mitotic index ~20 fold.
source: Exposure of wild-type MEFs to nocodazole for 6 hr. increased mitotic index ~20 fold, reflecting checkpoint-dependent detection of microtubule depolymerization and imposition of cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is supported by phospho-Histone H3 staining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The increase in mitotic index in wild-type MEFs exposed to nocodazole reflects checkpoint-dependent detection of microtubule depolymerization and imposition of cell cycle arrest.
source: Exposure of wild-type MEFs to nocodazole for 6 hr. increased mitotic index ~20 fold, reflecting checkpoint-dependent detection of microtubule depolymerization and imposition of cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is inferred from established knowledge about SAC function and nocodazole action.

claim: When Mad2l1Δ/Δ MEFS were exposed to nocodazole, only a modest increase in mitotic index was observed.
source: In contrast, when Mad2l1Δ/Δ MEFS were exposed to nocodazole, only a modest increase in mitotic index was observed, consistent with a loss of SAC–mediated mitotic delay (Figure 4B and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-Histone H3 staining data shown in Figure 4B and time-lapse imaging in Video 1.

claim: The modest increase in mitotic index in Mad2l1Δ/Δ MEFS exposed to nocodazole is consistent with a loss of SAC–mediated mitotic delay.
source: In contrast, when Mad2l1Δ/Δ MEFS were exposed to nocodazole, only a modest increase in mitotic index was observed, consistent with a loss of SAC–mediated mitotic delay (Figure 4B and Video 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison to wild-type MEFs and knowledge of SAC function.

claim: When wild type mice were injected with Paclitaxel, the fraction of phospho-H3 positive CD4+CD8+ thymocytes increased 6-fold.
source: When wild type and Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice were injected with the microtubule stabilizing drug Paclitaxel, the fraction of phospho-H3 positive CD4+CD8+ thymocytes (the most rapidly dividing thymic population) increased 6-fold in Mad2l1-sufficient animals but only 2.5-fold in Mad2l1-null animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-H3 staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice were injected with Paclitaxel, the fraction of phospho-H3 positive CD4+CD8+ thymocytes increased only 2.5-fold.
source: When wild type and Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice were injected with the microtubule stabilizing drug Paclitaxel, the fraction of phospho-H3 positive CD4+CD8+ thymocytes (the most rapidly dividing thymic population) increased 6-fold in Mad2l1-sufficient animals but only 2.5-fold in Mad2l1-null animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by phospho-H3 staining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mitotic checkpoint is functionally impaired in Mad2l1Δ/Δ thymocytes in vivo.
source: Thus, the mitotic checkpoint is functionally impaired in Mad2l1Δ/Δ thymocytes in vivo, consistent with loss of expression of a protein required for the spindle assembly checkpoint protein.
evidence: This is concluded from the reduced response to Paclitaxel in Mad2l1-deleted thymocytes.

claim: Loss of SAC function is compatible with rapid growth of both liquid and solid tumors in the mouse.
source: We conclude that loss of SAC function is compatible with rapid growth of both liquid and solid tumors in the mouse.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of rapidly growing T-ALLs and HCCs in Mad2l1-deleted mice.

claim: T-ALLs had a median of 3 whole chromosome loss or gain events per tumor.
source: T-ALLs had a median of 3 whole chromosome loss or gain events per tumor, whereas HCCs had a median of 2 (Figure 5A, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: HCCs had a median of 2 whole chromosome loss or gain events per tumor.
source: T-ALLs had a median of 3 whole chromosome loss or gain events per tumor, whereas HCCs had a median of 2 (Figure 5A, p>0.05).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of Chr13 was frequent in both T-ALL and HCC tumor types.
source: Loss of Chr13 was frequent in both tumor types (Figure 5B,C; green point in Figure 5C) as was gain of Chr15 (Figure 5B,C; red point in Figure 5C) which was also the most common whole-chromosome aneuploidy overall.
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Gain of Chr15 was frequent in both T-ALL and HCC tumor types.
source: Loss of Chr13 was frequent in both tumor types (Figure 5B,C; green point in Figure 5C) as was gain of Chr15 (Figure 5B,C; red point in Figure 5C) which was also the most common whole-chromosome aneuploidy overall.
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Gain of Chr15 was the most common whole-chromosome aneuploidy overall.
source: Loss of Chr13 was frequent in both tumor types (Figure 5B,C; green point in Figure 5C) as was gain of Chr15 (Figure 5B,C; red point in Figure 5C) which was also the most common whole-chromosome aneuploidy overall.
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: T-ALLs frequently gained Chr4 and Chr12.
source: Chromosomes also exhibited tissue-specific patterns of loss and gain: T-ALLs frequently gained Chr4 and Chr12 while HCCs lost these chromosomes (Figure 5B,C; Chr4: p<0.001, Chr12: p<0.01, blue points in 4E).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5B and C with statistical analysis.

claim: HCCs lost Chr4 and Chr12.
source: Chromosomes also exhibited tissue-specific patterns of loss and gain: T-ALLs frequently gained Chr4 and Chr12 while HCCs lost these chromosomes (Figure 5B,C; Chr4: p<0.001, Chr12: p<0.01, blue points in 4E).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5B and C with statistical analysis.

claim: Chr18 exhibited preferential gain in HCCs but loss in T-ALLs.
source: In contrast, Chr18 exhibited preferential gain in HCCs but loss in T-ALLs (Figure 5B,C; p<0.001, blue points in Figure 5C; aCGH of individual tumors is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A for T-ALLs and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B for HCCs).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5B and C with statistical analysis.

claim: On a per-chromosome basis there was statistically significant correlation between chromosome ploidy and levels of mRNA expression from genes expressed on that chromosome.
source: One known effect of aneuploidy is to alter mRNA expression through gene dosage. On a per-chromosome basis we observed statistically significant correlation between chromosome ploidy and levels of mRNA expression from genes expressed on that chromosome (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The genes that were differentially expressed in HCC and T-ALL were not the same.
source: However, the genes that were differentially expressed in HCC and T-ALL were not the same.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis comparing the two tumor types.

claim: Even for genes expressed on Chr15, which was gained in both HCC and T-ALL, the differentially expressed genes were not the same.
source: This was true even for genes expressed on Chr15, which was gained in both HCC and T-ALL (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The only common pathways affected in T-ALLs and HCC were metabolic pathways.
source: When we used Webgestalt (Zhang et al., 2005) to determine whether the same pathways were affected in T-ALLs and HCC, the only common denominators were metabolic pathways, in agreement with earlier findings showing that aneuploidy disrupts metabolism in multiple organisms (NCBI GEO GSE63689) (Williams et al., 2008; Torres et al., 2007; Foijer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis and citations to previous work.

claim: Aneuploidy disrupts metabolism in multiple organisms.
source: When we used Webgestalt (Zhang et al., 2005) to determine whether the same pathways were affected in T-ALLs and HCC, the only common denominators were metabolic pathways, in agreement with earlier findings showing that aneuploidy disrupts metabolism in multiple organisms (NCBI GEO GSE63689) (Williams et al., 2008; Torres et al., 2007; Foijer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Deletion of Mad2l1 results in loss and gain of whole chromosomes in both HCC and T-ALL.
source: We conclude that deletion of Mad2l1 results in loss and gain of whole chromosomes in both HCC and T-ALL but that the pattern of gain and loss is tissue specific, most likely due to changes in gene expression that are themselves tissue-specific.
evidence: This is concluded from the aCGH data showing chromosome alterations.

claim: The pattern of chromosome gain and loss in Mad2l1-deleted tumors is tissue specific.
source: We conclude that deletion of Mad2l1 results in loss and gain of whole chromosomes in both HCC and T-ALL but that the pattern of gain and loss is tissue specific, most likely due to changes in gene expression that are themselves tissue-specific.
evidence: This is concluded from the aCGH data showing different patterns in different tumor types.

claim: The tissue-specific pattern of chromosome gain and loss is most likely due to changes in gene expression that are themselves tissue-specific.
source: We conclude that deletion of Mad2l1 results in loss and gain of whole chromosomes in both HCC and T-ALL but that the pattern of gain and loss is tissue specific, most likely due to changes in gene expression that are themselves tissue-specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of tissue-specific chromosome alterations and differential gene expression.

claim: Even when the same chromosome is gained in HCC and T-ALL, the genes that exhibit differential expression are not the same.
source: Moreover, even when the same chromosome is gained in HCC and T-ALL, the genes that exhibit differential expression are not the same.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis of Chr15 shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ~30% of T-ALLs carried a 1–8 gene deletion spanning Pten.
source: For both T-ALL and HCC aCGH revealed recurrent copy number variants (CNVs), focal changes in chromosome structure, some of which included known oncogenes and tumor suppressors. We found that ~30% of T-ALLs carried a 1–8 gene deletion spanning Pten (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), a negative regulator of the PI3 kinase and 5–10% of HCCs carried an amplification in Met, a known oncogene in human HCC (Zender et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pten is a negative regulator of the PI3 kinase.
source: We found that ~30% of T-ALLs carried a 1–8 gene deletion spanning Pten (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), a negative regulator of the PI3 kinase and 5–10% of HCCs carried an amplification in Met, a known oncogene in human HCC (Zender et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Pten function.

claim: 5–10% of HCCs carried an amplification in Met.
source: We found that ~30% of T-ALLs carried a 1–8 gene deletion spanning Pten (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), a negative regulator of the PI3 kinase and 5–10% of HCCs carried an amplification in Met, a known oncogene in human HCC (Zender et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Met is a known oncogene in human HCC.
source: We found that ~30% of T-ALLs carried a 1–8 gene deletion spanning Pten (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), a negative regulator of the PI3 kinase and 5–10% of HCCs carried an amplification in Met, a known oncogene in human HCC (Zender et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Met RNA and protein were over-expressed in HCCs with Met amplification.
source: In the latter case, we confirmed that Met RNA and protein were over-expressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and Western blotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: No consistently amplified or deleted genes were common to both thymus and liver tumors.
source: We detected no consistently amplified or deleted genes common to both thymus and liver tumors: three possible candidates uncovered by aCGH proved to be artifacts arising from our use of a mixed 129 x C57BL/6 background (Boyden and Dietrich, 2006) (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is concluded from aCGH analysis and identification of artifacts.

claim: The overall structure and pattern of gene amplifications and deletions appeared to differ in T-ALL and HCC tumor types.
source: Moreover, the overall structure and pattern of gene amplifications and deletions appeared to differ in the two tumor types.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of CNV characteristics.

claim: Focal CNVs were more frequent in T-ALL than HCC.
source: Focal CNVs were more frequent in T-ALL than HCC: T-ALLs carried a median of 29 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~40 genes per CNV whereas HCCs carried ~20 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~2–3 genes (both differences were statistically significant, ~p< 0.05 and p<0.01 respectively; Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I and J with statistical testing.

claim: T-ALLs carried a median of 29 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~40 genes per CNV.
source: Focal CNVs were more frequent in T-ALL than HCC: T-ALLs carried a median of 29 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~40 genes per CNV whereas HCCs carried ~20 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~2–3 genes (both differences were statistically significant, ~p< 0.05 and p<0.01 respectively; Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: HCCs carried ~20 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~2–3 genes.
source: Focal CNVs were more frequent in T-ALL than HCC: T-ALLs carried a median of 29 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~40 genes per CNV whereas HCCs carried ~20 CNVs per tumor with an average size of ~2–3 genes (both differences were statistically significant, ~p< 0.05 and p<0.01 respectively; Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: T-ALLs appear to be clonal based on TCR sequence.
source: We note a potential complication in the interpretation of this data. Whereas T-ALLs appear to be clonal based on TCR sequence HCCs are likely to be polyclonal even after physical dissociation of tumor masses.
evidence: This is supported by TCR analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: HCCs are likely to be polyclonal even after physical dissociation of tumor masses.
source: We note a potential complication in the interpretation of this data. Whereas T-ALLs appear to be clonal based on TCR sequence HCCs are likely to be polyclonal even after physical dissociation of tumor masses.
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of solid tumors and the presence of mixed genotypes.

claim: Mice lacking Mad2l1 in hepatocytes exhibited a characteristic progression from regeneration nodules to HCA and then HCC.
source: Mice lacking Mad2l1 in hepatocytes exhibited a characteristic progression from regeneration nodules to HCA and then HCC.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis at different time points shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chromosomes 15, 16, and 18 were frequently gained in HCC.
source: Chromosomes 15, 16, and 18 were frequently gained in HCC (as described above) and also in HCA, although signals were weaker in HCAs implying that only a subset of cells had undergone chromosome gain events (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Chromosomes 15, 16, and 18 were also gained in HCA, although signals were weaker implying that only a subset of cells had undergone chromosome gain events.
source: Chromosomes 15, 16, and 18 were frequently gained in HCC (as described above) and also in HCA, although signals were weaker in HCAs implying that only a subset of cells had undergone chromosome gain events (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 6A and inferred from the weaker signals.

claim: HCA appeared more aneuploid than normal tissue.
source: Overall, HCA appeared more aneuploid than normal tissue and HCC more aneuploid than HCA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HCC appeared more aneuploid than HCA.
source: Overall, HCA appeared more aneuploid than normal tissue and HCC more aneuploid than HCA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Two pairs of HCA and HCC tumors were strongly related based on CNV similarity.
source: We identified two pairs of HCA and HCC tumors that were strongly related and found that the two HCCs that arose in a single mouse were also strongly related (relative to tumors from different animals; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by Jaccard Index analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The two HCCs that arose in a single mouse were strongly related.
source: We identified two pairs of HCA and HCC tumors that were strongly related and found that the two HCCs that arose in a single mouse were also strongly related (relative to tumors from different animals; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by Jaccard Index analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: In three animals HCA and HCCs were weakly related.
source: In three animals HCA and HCCs were weakly related and in four animals we did not detect significant similarity (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by Jaccard Index analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: In four animals HCA and HCCs did not show significant similarity.
source: In three animals HCA and HCCs were weakly related and in four animals we did not detect significant similarity (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by Jaccard Index analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: Tumor pairs from the same mouse were significantly more similar to each other than to tumors from other mice.
source: In aggregate, tumor pairs from the same mouse were significantly more similar to each other than to tumors from other mice, but only 10–20% of CNVs overlapped among benign and malignant tumors from the same animal.
evidence: This is concluded from the Jaccard Index analysis.

claim: Only 10–20% of CNVs overlapped among benign and malignant tumors from the same animal.
source: In aggregate, tumor pairs from the same mouse were significantly more similar to each other than to tumors from other mice, but only 10–20% of CNVs overlapped among benign and malignant tumors from the same animal.
evidence: This is concluded from the Jaccard Index analysis.

claim: HCC can evolve from HCA in the mouse model.
source: We conclude that HCC can indeed evolve from HCA in our mouse model but that HCA may not be a necessary precursor to HCC.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of related HCA and HCC pairs.

claim: HCA may not be a necessary precursor to HCC.
source: We conclude that HCC can indeed evolve from HCA in our mouse model but that HCA may not be a necessary precursor to HCC.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that some HCCs are not related to HCAs.

claim: Progression from HCA to HCC and clonal evolution are accompanied by ongoing gain and loss of whole chromosomes and CNVs.
source: Nonetheless, our data clearly demonstrate the possibility of evolution from HCA to HCC in a single animal and of a single HCC into a macroscopically distinct HCC in the same organ. Both progression and clonal evolution are accompanied by ongoing gain and loss of whole chromosomes and CNVs.
evidence: This is concluded from the CNV analysis of related tumors.

claim: No chromosomal abnormalities were observed in T-cells from wild-type thymi by single-cell sequencing.
source: As expected, no chromosomal abnormalities were observed in T-cells from wild-type thymi (Figure 6C) but extensive aneuploidy was evident in 3 T-ALL samples (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Extensive aneuploidy was evident in 3 T-ALL samples by single-cell sequencing.
source: As expected, no chromosomal abnormalities were observed in T-cells from wild-type thymi (Figure 6C) but extensive aneuploidy was evident in 3 T-ALL samples (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Most cells from all three T-ALLs subjected to single-cell analysis had gained Chr. 14 and 15.
source: Most cells from all three T-ALLs subjected to single-cell analysis had gained Chr. 14 and 15 (Figure 6D–F) and in one of two tumors examined, a preponderance of cells had gained Chr. 1, 2, 4, 5, and 17 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: In one T-ALL tumor, a preponderance of cells had gained Chr. 1, 2, 4, 5, and 17.
source: Most cells from all three T-ALLs subjected to single-cell analysis had gained Chr. 14 and 15 (Figure 6D–F) and in one of two tumors examined, a preponderance of cells had gained Chr. 1, 2, 4, 5, and 17 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Changes in the ploidy of other chromosomes appeared random in T-ALL single cells.
source: In contrast, changes in the ploidy of other chromosomes appeared random: > 70% of the cells in a single T-ALL had unique karyotypes.
evidence: This is concluded from single-cell sequencing data showing diverse karyotypes.

claim: > 70% of the cells in a single T-ALL had unique karyotypes.
source: In contrast, changes in the ploidy of other chromosomes appeared random: > 70% of the cells in a single T-ALL had unique karyotypes.
evidence: This is concluded from single-cell sequencing data.

claim: Intratumor differences in karyotype were evidenced by high heterogeneity scores for all three T-ALLs.
source: Intratumor differences in karyotype were further evidenced by high heterogeneity scores for all three T-ALLs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by heterogeneity score analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Heterogeneity scores for Mad2l1-null T-ALLs were higher than those of T-ALLs expressing truncated Mps1.
source: These scores were also higher than those of T-ALLs expressing truncated Mps1 (Foijer et al., 2014; Bakker et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous data supported by citations.

claim: T-ALLs were clonal based on TCR loci.
source: Because T-ALLs were clonal based on TCR loci, the most likely explanation for intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity is ongoing chromosome loss and gain, presumably due to loss of SAC function.
evidence: This is supported by TCR analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The most likely explanation for intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity in T-ALLs is ongoing chromosome loss and gain.
