source: Because T-ALLs were clonal based on TCR loci, the most likely explanation for intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity is ongoing chromosome loss and gain, presumably due to loss of SAC function.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of clonality and karyotypic heterogeneity.

claim: Intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity in T-ALLs is presumably due to loss of SAC function.
source: Because T-ALLs were clonal based on TCR loci, the most likely explanation for intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity is ongoing chromosome loss and gain, presumably due to loss of SAC function.
evidence: This is inferred from the known role of SAC in maintaining chromosome stability.

claim: Human cancers in the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) have an abnormal pan-cancer karyotype involving Chrs. 7, 20 (frequently gained) and Chrs. 10, 13, 22 (frequently lost).
source: Human cancers in the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) have previously been reported to have an abnormal pan-cancer karyotype involving Chrs. 7, 20 (which are frequently gained) and Chrs. 10, 13, 22 (which are frequently lost) (Davoli et al., 2013; Nicholson and Cimini, 2013) as well as tissue-specific changes in chromosome ploidy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous analysis of TCGA data.

claim: Human cancers in TCGA show tissue-specific changes in chromosome ploidy.
source: Human cancers in the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) have previously been reported to have an abnormal pan-cancer karyotype involving Chrs. 7, 20 (which are frequently gained) and Chrs. 10, 13, 22 (which are frequently lost) (Davoli et al., 2013; Nicholson and Cimini, 2013) as well as tissue-specific changes in chromosome ploidy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous analysis of TCGA data.

claim: In human HCCs, chromosomes Chr1q and Chr8q are commonly gained.
source: In human HCCs, chromosomes Chr1q and Chr8q are commonly gained and Chr8p lost (Figure 7; top panel), an event that has been associated with worse clinical outcomes (Emi et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7 and citation.

claim: In human HCCs, Chr8p is commonly lost.
source: In human HCCs, chromosomes Chr1q and Chr8q are commonly gained and Chr8p lost (Figure 7; top panel), an event that has been associated with worse clinical outcomes (Emi et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7 and citation.

claim: Gain of Chr8q and loss of Chr8p in human HCC has been associated with worse clinical outcomes.
source: In human HCCs, chromosomes Chr1q and Chr8q are commonly gained and Chr8p lost (Figure 7; top panel), an event that has been associated with worse clinical outcomes (Emi et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical studies.

claim: Human 8q is related to murine Chr. 15.
source: Human 8q is related to murine Chr. 15, which we find frequently gained in Mad2l1-null HCCs (Hertz et al., 2008; Guan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to synteny studies.

claim: Murine Chr. 15 is frequently gained in Mad2l1-null HCCs.
source: Human 8q is related to murine Chr. 15, which we find frequently gained in Mad2l1-null HCCs (Hertz et al., 2008; Guan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data from the manuscript.

claim: Similar karyotypic abnormalities are found in HCC and breast cancer.
source: Similar karyotypic abnormalities are found in HCC and breast cancer (Figure 7, top panel), consistent with the existence of a pan-cancer karyotype.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The similarity in karyotypic abnormalities between HCC and breast cancer is consistent with the existence of a pan-cancer karyotype.
source: Similar karyotypic abnormalities are found in HCC and breast cancer (Figure 7, top panel), consistent with the existence of a pan-cancer karyotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar patterns across cancer types.

claim: Non-epithelial cancers exhibit a very different karyotypic pattern than carcinomas.
source: However, non-epithelial cancers exhibit a very different karyotypic pattern than carcinomas (compare upper and lower panels Figure 7) and see also (Zack et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7 and citation.

claim: Epithelial and non-epithelial human cancers are similar to Mad2l1-null HCC and T-ALL in having distinct karyotypes.
source: Thus, epithelial and non-epithelial human cancers are similar to Mad2l1-null HCC and T-ALL in having distinct karyotypes, perhaps because they experience different selective pressures.
evidence: This is concluded from comparison of human and mouse tumor karyotypes.

claim: Epithelial and non-epithelial cancers may have distinct karyotypes because they experience different selective pressures.
source: Thus, epithelial and non-epithelial human cancers are similar to Mad2l1-null HCC and T-ALL in having distinct karyotypes, perhaps because they experience different selective pressures.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of distinct karyotypes.

claim: Deletion of both Mad2l1 and Trp53 in T-cells results in T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma and death of animals within 4–5 months.
source: Deletion of both Mad2l1 and Trp53 in T-cells (promoted by Lck-Cre) results in T-cell acute lymphoblastic lymphoma and death of animals within 4–5 months as a result of grossly enlarged thymi and dyspnea.
evidence: This is supported by survival data and pathological observations.

claim: Mice that lose Trp53 and Mad2l1 in hepatocytes initially develop regeneration nodules.
source: Mice that lose Trp53 and Mad2l1 in hepatocytes (promoted by Alb-Cre) initially develop regeneration nodules, a sign of on-going liver repair, then hepatocellular carcinoma, a benign liver tumor and finally hepatocellular carcinoma, an aggressive liver cancer resulting in death between 12–15 months of age.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis at different time points.

claim: HCCs lacking Mad2l1 grow rapidly for solid tumors, with an estimated doubling time of 28 days.
source: HCCs lacking Mad2l1 grow rapidly for solid tumors, with an estimated doubling time of 28 days.
evidence: This is supported by MRI measurements shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The age of tumor onset and of death in single and double knockout animals strongly suggests that tumorigenesis is driven by the compound effects of Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss.
source: The age of tumor onset and of death in single and double knockout animals strongly suggests that tumorigenesis is driven by the compound effects of Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data comparing different genotypes.

claim: Liver tumors can arise in mice that are deleted for Mad2l1 alone.
source: However, liver tumors can also arise in mice that are deleted for Mad2l1 alone, showing that Trp53 deletion is not a pre-requisite for tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of tumors in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f animals.

claim: Trp53 deletion is not a pre-requisite for tumorigenesis in Mad2l1-deleted hepatocytes.
source: However, liver tumors can also arise in mice that are deleted for Mad2l1 alone, showing that Trp53 deletion is not a pre-requisite for tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of tumors in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f animals.

claim: Hepatocytes are normally polyploid, potentially making them more tolerant of changes in chromosome number than other cell types.
source: This may relate to the fact that hepatocytes are normally polyploid, and thus, potentially more tolerant of changes in chromosome number than other cell types.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known polyploidy of hepatocytes.

claim: Loss of Mad2l1 in adult tissues can be strongly oncogenic.
source: We conclude that loss of Mad2l1 in adult tissues can be strongly oncogenic, in contrast to heterozygous Mad2l1 deletion, which is only weakly cancer promoting (Michel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is concluded from the tumor data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Heterozygous Mad2l1 deletion is only weakly cancer promoting.
source: We conclude that loss of Mad2l1 in adult tissues can be strongly oncogenic, in contrast to heterozygous Mad2l1 deletion, which is only weakly cancer promoting (Michel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mad2l1f/f mice having a range of Trp53 genotypes represent a valuable tool for studying the SAC in vivo.
source: Mad2l1f/f mice having a range of Trp53 genotypes therefore represent a valuable tool for studying the SAC in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the mouse model developed in the manuscript.

claim: The rapid growth of Mad2l1-deficient liquid and solid tumors stands in contrast to previous data showing that Mad2l1 is essential for the survival of cancer cell lines and for development of early mouse embryos.
source: The rapid growth of Mad2l1-deficient liquid and solid tumors stands in contrast to previous data showing that Mad2l1 is essential for the survival of cancer cell lines and for development of early mouse embryos (Kops et al., 2004; Dobles et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings supported by citations.

claim: Mad2l1 loss substantially accelerates tumor development in Trp53-positive and/or mutant backgrounds.
source: Mad2l1 loss substantially accelerates tumor development in Trp53-positive and/or mutant backgrounds (depending on cell type) emphasizing that checkpoint inactivation and CIN are not just tolerated by cells, they accelerate disease onset in animals already mutant for a potent tumor suppresser.
evidence: This is supported by survival data comparing different genotypes.

claim: Checkpoint inactivation and CIN accelerate disease onset in animals already mutant for a potent tumor suppressor.
source: Mad2l1 loss substantially accelerates tumor development in Trp53-positive and/or mutant backgrounds (depending on cell type) emphasizing that checkpoint inactivation and CIN are not just tolerated by cells, they accelerate disease onset in animals already mutant for a potent tumor suppresser.
evidence: This is concluded from the synergistic effects of Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss.

claim: The near-complete absence of response to nocodazole in Mad2l1-deleted MEFs is consistent with checkpoint inactivation.
source: In cultured MEFs and thymocytes assayed in vivo, the microtubule poisons nocodazole and taxol provoke a significantly weaker cell cycle arrest than in wild-type cells. The near-complete absence of response to nocodazole in MEFs is consistent with checkpoint inactivation but in vivo experiments with thymocytes reveal partial responsiveness to taxol.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional assay results.

claim: Checkpoint deficiency is tolerated by basal epidermal skin cells but is lethal to hair follicle stem cells.
source: Parallel experiments in our labs have shown that checkpoint deficiency is also tolerated by basal epidermal skin cells but is lethal to hair follicle stem cells (Foijer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: SAC inactivation is compatible with proliferation of some cell types but not others.
source: These data established that SAC inactivation is compatible with proliferation of some cell types but not others.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential tolerance of different cell types to Mad2l1 deletion.

claim: Most T-ALLs are clonal and show no evidence of Mad2l1 expression.
source: Since most T-ALLs are clonal and show no evidence of Mad2l1 expression, they must arise from a single checkpoint-null initiating cell following many rounds of cell division.
evidence: This is supported by TCR analysis and Mad2l1 expression data.

claim: T-ALLs must arise from a single checkpoint-null initiating cell following many rounds of cell division.
source: Since most T-ALLs are clonal and show no evidence of Mad2l1 expression, they must arise from a single checkpoint-null initiating cell following many rounds of cell division.
evidence: This is inferred from the clonality and lack of Mad2l1 expression.

claim: In Mad2l1-deficient HCCs we observe fewer and smaller CNV lesions than in T-ALL.
source: The consequences of Mad2l1 inactivation for chromosome structure also appear to differ with cell type: in Mad2l1-deficient HCCs we observe fewer and smaller lesions that in T-ALL.
evidence: This is supported by CNV analysis shown in Figure 5I and J.

claim: Loss of Mad2l1 creates a mutator phenotype in the absence of an overt oncogenic driver.
source: Loss of Mad2l1 creates a mutator phenotype in the absence of an overt oncogenic driver.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation of extensive genomic alterations in Mad2l1-deleted tumors.

claim: Large-scale genomic analysis of Mad2l1-deficient tumors may be useful for identifying new oncogenes and tumor suppressors.
source: Large-scale genomic analysis of Mad2l1-deficient tumors may be a generally useful means for identifying new oncogenes and tumor suppressors as well as genes (such as Trp53) whose mutation tolerizes cells to checkpoint loss and aneuploidy (Torres et al., 2010; Fujiwara et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential utility of the model.

claim: Mad2l1f/f animals may be useful in studying the role of genomic instability in drug resistance and tumor recurrence.
source: Mad2l1f/f animals may also be useful in studying the role of genomic instability in drug resistance and tumor recurrence (Burrell and Swanton, 2014b, 2014a) and in the clonal evolution of tumors (Sotillo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential utility of the model supported by citations.

claim: Single-cell sequencing of T-ALLs from Mad2l1-deficient mice reveals extensive aneuploidy and intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity.
source: Single-cell sequencing of T-ALLs from Mad2l1-deficient mice reveals extensive aneuploidy and intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell sequencing data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: In some animals with liver cancer, there was evidence of clonal progression from HCA to HCC.
source: In some animals with liver cancer, we found evidence of clonal progression from HCA to HCC as well as genetic progression among physically distinct HCCs in a single animal.
evidence: This is supported by CNV similarity analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: There was evidence of genetic progression among physically distinct HCCs in a single animal.
source: In some animals with liver cancer, we found evidence of clonal progression from HCA to HCC as well as genetic progression among physically distinct HCCs in a single animal.
evidence: This is supported by CNV similarity analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The data are consistent with findings from ultra-deep whole genome sequencing of lung cancers demonstrating extensive intra-tumor heterogeneity.
source: Our data are also consistent with findings from ultra-deep whole genome sequencing of lung cancers demonstrating extensive intra-tumor heterogeneity at the level of point mutations and structural chromosome abnormalities (de Bruin et al., 2014; Gerlinger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings supported by citations.

claim: The average karyotype of Mad2l1-deficient T-ALL and HCC cell populations involves pan-cancer and tissue-specific patterns of whole chromosome loss and gain.
source: In Mad2l1-deficient murine T-ALLs, HCAs and HCCs, the average karyotype of cell populations is shown by aCGH to involve pan-cancer and tissue-specific patterns of whole chromosome loss and gain.
evidence: This is supported by aCGH data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Karyotypic variation results in differential loss and gain of oncogenes and tumor suppressors.
source: Karyotypic variation presumably results in differential loss and gain of oncogenes and tumor suppressors as discussed above, but it also causes large-scale changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed CNVs affecting known cancer genes.

claim: Karyotypic variation causes large-scale changes in gene expression.
source: Karyotypic variation presumably results in differential loss and gain of oncogenes and tumor suppressors as discussed above, but it also causes large-scale changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by expression analysis showing correlation with chromosome ploidy.

claim: Genes located on chromosomes with abnormal ploidy generally change in levels of expression.
source: In general, genes that are located on chromosomes with abnormal ploidy also change in levels of expression, but even when T-ALL and HCC experience the same change in ploidy for a particular chromosome, GSEA shows that differentially expressed genes do not overlap.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Karyotypic selection is imposed both at the level of structural rearrangements in specific genes and broad changes in gene expression.
source: We therefore speculate that karyotypic selection is imposed both at the level of structural rearrangements in specific genes and broad changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed patterns of CNVs and gene expression changes.

claim: Selection in the face of ongoing CIN contrasts with a model of genome restabilization in which CIN is a transient phenomenon.
source: Selection in the face of ongoing CIN contrasts with a model of a genome restabilization in which CIN is a transient phenomenon and tumor karyotype maintained because aneuploid or structurally abnormal chromosomes are subsequently transmitted with good fidelity.
evidence: This is a comparison to an alternative model discussed in the introduction.
